title: Geremie Barmé on the ‘Other China’ - The Wire China
gist: Sinologist Geremie Barmé argues Xi Jinping's Politburo is the last gasp of the Cultural Revolution generation, still obsessed with the Maoist concept of 'bourgeois rights', and that Xi has succeeded at the balancing act of reconciling Maoist top-down control with reformist commercialization at devastating social cost. He also argues Xi is far more powerful than Mao ever was, that the 2018 constitutional revision gave him 'terminal tenure', and that the deliberate destruction of factional signalling and Hong Kong's publishing industry has left outsiders with almost no reliable read on elite Chinese politics.

themes.theme: Cultural Revolution DNA in the current Politburo

insights.claim: China's current Politburo is composed of people from the ex-Red Guard generation, making the present Chinese government the last surviving political expression of the Cultural Revolution era rather than a purely post-reform technocracy.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Policy toward private wealth and consumerism is generational and ideological, not tactical — expect it to persist until this cohort physically exits the stage.
insights.quote: The present Chinese government is the last gasp of the Cultural Revolution era.
insights.locator: How does this introduction to China... impact your China analysis now?

insights.claim: The Maoist concept of 'bourgeois rights' [资产阶级法权] — the idea that wage differentials, privilege systems and private property inevitably regenerate capitalism — sat at the core of both the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution and continues to obsess Xi Jinping and his colleagues today.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Explains recurring campaigns against wealth accumulation, platform billionaires and 'disorderly capital' as ideological rather than merely regulatory — a structural discount factor on Chinese private-sector equity.
insights.quote: The concept of ‘bourgeois rights’ [资产阶级法权] was at the core of the Cultural Revolution, the core of the Great Leap Forward, and the core idea that really continues to obsess Xi Jinping and colleagues today.

insights.claim: The 1975 campaign's own prediction — that failing to eliminate material privilege and private property would inevitably return China to a capitalist consumerist paradigm — turned out to be empirically correct, which is precisely why the doctrine retains force with the leadership.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Beijing's hardliners can point to a vindicated theory, which strengthens the internal case for periodic anti-consumerist and redistributive lurches.
insights.quote: Guess what? They were right!
insights.locator: Basically, this movement maintained

insights.claim: The Chinese party-state functions as an empire of hierarchy, language and control that polices the boundary between insiders and outsiders, and beneath the layer of state authoritarianism China remains a fundamentally 'semi-feudal' society.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Access, patronage and insider status — not formal rules — determine outcomes for firms and investors operating in China.
insights.quote: state authoritarianism aside, Chinese remains a ‘semi-feudal’ society
insights.locator: Apart from that, learning to appreciate the actual mechanics

insights.claim: In early 2013 Xi Jinping declared that the reform era of 1978–2008 must not be allowed to overwhelm and negate the Mao era of 1949–1978, setting the doctrinal frame for his entire tenure.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The 'two 30 years' doctrine is the published constraint on how far market liberalization can ever go under this leadership.
insights.quote: we must not allow the second 30-year period — the reform era from ’78 to 2008 — to overwhelm and negate the first 30 years — ’49 to ’78, that is the Mao era.
insights.locator: In early 2013, shortly after he came into power

insights.claim: Reading Xi's rule as a simple return to the Cultural Revolution is wrong; his actual project is to reconcile the irreconcilable by adjudicating between authoritarian top-down control and innovative economic reformist commercialization.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Bets premised on ideological self-destruction of the Chinese economy misread the model; commercial innovation is deliberately preserved inside the control architecture.
insights.quote: to adjudicate between authoritarian top-down control and innovative economic reformist commercialization
insights.locator: Some commentators, both Chinese and international

insights.claim: Judged against China's stated grand project of becoming wealthy and powerful, the last ten to fifteen years under Xi have been quite successful — a success purchased with social repression, violence toward minorities and the suppression of civic aspirations.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Expect the leadership to defend continuity on results, not to be forced into liberalization by any internal performance audit.
insights.quote: The social cost of this success, however, is devastating: social repression, violence toward minorities and marginalized groups and the restrictions on people’s legitimate civic aspirations to have a say in their lives.
insights.locator: The social cost of this success

insights.claim: Xi Jinping is expected to argue the wealth-and-power success record directly to his comrades in the coming year as he navigates toward yet another term in power.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Watch the run-up to the next Party leadership round for performance-legitimacy messaging as the tell on succession dynamics.
insights.locator: I daresay Xi Jinping will be making exactly this case

themes.theme: Terminal tenure and the friability of one-man rule

insights.claim: The 2018 revision of China's constitution effectively gave Xi Jinping 'terminal tenure' — an open-ended hold on the party-state-army leadership rather than a conventional term-limited presidency.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Model Chinese political risk as an indefinite single-principal regime; there is no scheduled transition date to trade around.
insights.quote: since the 2018 revision of the constitution, Xi effectively enjoys “terminal tenure”
insights.locator: I have long said that

insights.claim: The common media claim that Xi is the most powerful Chinese leader since Mao understates the case — he is far more powerful than Mao ever was, holds more titles than the Qianlong Emperor, and has a handpicked Politburo, Military Commission and State Council.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Policy reversals require Xi's own change of mind; institutional veto points that could slow a bad decision no longer exist.
insights.quote: of course he’s much more powerful than Mao ever was. He has more titles than the Qianlong Emperor.
insights.locator: People in the media always talk about Xi

insights.claim: Xi's need to repeatedly hand-pick and re-pick his military commanders is evidence that his power is friable rather than Stalin-absolute, and that powerful provincial and military figures still have to be courted and kept happy even if they cannot challenge him.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Repeated PLA leadership churn is a readable stress indicator on regime stability — track purges of military appointees rather than official rhetoric.
insights.quote: Of course, Caesar can’t trust the praetorian guard.
insights.locator: Yet, if he had the kind of absolute power enjoyed by Stalin

insights.claim: Xi deliberately destroyed the observability of Chinese elite politics: he formally banned factional activity in 2013, purged those engaged in it, and imposed disciplinary rules making it illegal for retired senior cadres to comment on central party policy.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Faction-based China analysis is now largely unfalsifiable noise; discount research products that claim to map Beijing power blocs.
insights.quote: He formally banned factional activity
insights.locator: one of the things Xi Jinping did when he got into power in 2013

insights.claim: The shutdown from July 2019 of Hong Kong's independent media and publishing industry destroyed the essential outlet that had, since 1949, carried rumors, gossip and speculation originating in Beijing to the outside world.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The information channel that used to price Chinese political surprise is gone — expect more discontinuous, unhedgeable policy shocks out of Beijing.
insights.locator: from July 2019, his myrmidons effectively shut down

themes.theme: Maple Bridge: the surveillance template and its early tells

insights.claim: Xi Jinping revived the Maoist 'Maple Bridge Experience' — social policing through networks of informants, vigilantes and front-line organs of the people's dictatorship — as security policy for the 2008 Olympic year after being lobbied by local cadres while running Zhejiang.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: China's modern surveillance apparatus has a documented pre-2012 pilot; it is a deep institutional commitment, not a recent tech-enabled improvisation.
insights.quote: Maple Bridge was a form of social policing that relied on networks of informants, vigilantes and the front line “organs of the people’s dictatorship”.
insights.locator: Then in 2008, as a member of the Politburo

insights.claim: Xi's hardline direction was legible years before he took power — via leaked hardline internal speeches during the 2008 Olympic Torch Relay and Wu Bangguo's March 2011 'Five Don'ts' speech renouncing democracy and press freedom.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Internal speeches and second-tier leaders' doctrinal statements are the leading indicator of Chinese policy regime shifts; public reassurance is the lagging one.
insights.locator: Xi also made a number of secret internal speeches

insights.claim: Xi institutionalized his personal control by appointing himself chair of a series of new guiding committees immediately on taking power, an effective auto-golpe by the Party head against the state apparatus.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Decision-making runs through Party leading groups, not ministries — state-level technocrats are not the counterparties that matter.
insights.quote: That’s when I started calling him the “Chairman of Everything”.
insights.locator: Very soon after he came to power

insights.claim: Under Xi the media control doctrine was restated in explicitly Maoist terms, reviving the slogan that the Communist Party rules everything and coining the line that the media has only one surname and that surname is 'The Party'.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Chinese domestic media and data releases should be read as policy instruments, not as independent information.
insights.quote: the media has only one surname and that surname is ‘The Party’.
insights.locator: In 2016, Xi Jinping even revived the dreadful Mao slogan

insights.claim: Beneath the Party overculture there persists an 'other China' of creators, writers, translators and performers that is irrepressible, vocal and optimistic, and which the Party overculture both dominates and feeds off.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Cultural and consumer dynamism in China is generated outside the state and survives crackdowns — a reason not to write off Chinese creative and consumer sectors entirely.
insights.quote: a world that is irrepressible, vocal, creative, and despite everything, somewhat upbeat, always optimistic
insights.locator: I eventually started referring to my experience

insights.claim: Chinese social space is not monotonically closing but oscillating — independent filmmaking, literature, poetry and gender debate continue because the Party, depending on its whims and needs, periodically allows room for them.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Treat Chinese regulatory and cultural crackdowns as cyclical swerves with reopening phases, not one-way ratchets.
insights.quote: This is what China is: a swerve to the left, a swerve to the right.
insights.locator: It flourishes in so many disparate ways

insights.claim: Xi Jinping has been more effective at clamping down on independent civil society than any other post-Mao Chinese leader.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Baseline expectations for civil-society-driven liberalization in China should be set lower than at any point since 1978.
insights.locator: Xi Jinping has been more successful in clamping down

themes.theme: Pax Xinensis, AI and the post-Xi undo

insights.claim: The future of Chinese repression is imagined not as crude Orwellian brutality but as a consumer-branded, AI-designed apparatus — luxury goods promoted by domestic and fellow-traveller influencers and available for frictionless online purchase and international delivery.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Watch the fusion of AI, e-commerce and influencer marketing with state control as a Chinese export category rather than a purely domestic phenomenon.
insights.quote: Under Pax Xinensis it is likely that the boot of power will be AI-designed footwear crafted from high-end materials and labour-farm leather.
insights.locator: In The Threnody of Tedium, I quoted George Orwell

insights.claim: Whoever follows Xi and his Red-Guard-era cohort — possibly decades away — will have to relitigate the 1980s battles against one-man rule, restoring collective leadership, limited terms for party leaders and internal Party democracy.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Any post-Xi liberalization is a decade-plus horizon and starts by undoing, not innovating — do not price a fast institutional normalization.
insights.locator: After Xi and his generation of Red-guard-era leaders

insights.claim: By overturning his predecessors' efforts to eliminate capricious one-man rule, Xi Jinping has reinserted pre-modern political practices into the twenty-first century and potentially condemned China to repeat the historical cycles the Communist Party claims to have escaped.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Succession crisis risk is structurally re-embedded in the Chinese system — a long-dated tail risk for anything with China exposure.
insights.quote: he has insinuated the practices of the past into the twenty-first-century. He has potentially condemned the country to repeat the very cycles of history from which the Communists boast that they have broken free.
insights.locator: The distaste I have for Xi Jinping

insights.claim: Economic change and China's social maturation will eventually push the country beyond the confines of strict command-and-control ideology regardless of how hard the current leadership pushes those policies.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The long-run bull case on China rests on social and economic maturation outrunning ideology, not on any policy pivot.

themes.theme: Taiwan and Hong Kong: the credibility of Beijing's guarantees

insights.claim: Taiwan's functioning democracy is an existential ideological threat to Beijing because it disproves the Party's claim that Chinese people and traditions make democratic life unviable — which is why the party-state is determined to see it snuffed out.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Taiwan risk is driven by regime legitimacy, not just territorial nationalism — it does not fade with economic pragmatism or de-escalation gestures.
insights.quote: Ideologically, and in practical political terms, Taiwan is an existential threat to Beijing.
insights.locator: as for the realization of democracy and an open society

insights.claim: Observers in Hong Kong concluded as early as the 1979 Deng–MacLehose meeting that the territory would eventually be treated like Tibet after the 1951 17-point agreement, because the Communists had already reneged on their democratic promises of the 1946–49 Civil War.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Beijing's written guarantees to autonomous jurisdictions have a documented history of expiry — price legal-regime risk in Hong Kong and any future arrangement accordingly.
insights.quote: We all felt Hong Kong would eventually be completely screwed over, treated like Tibet following the 17-point agreement of 1951, no matter how long it might take.
insights.locator: The second was that Deng Xiaoping met with the Governor MacLehose

insights.claim: Deng Xiaoping's March 1979 Four Cardinal Principles, announced alongside the jailing of Democracy Wall activist Wei Jingsheng for 15 years, permanently capped the possibility of substantive political evolution in China under the Party.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The political ceiling on Chinese reform was set in 1979, not 2013 — Xi is enforcing a constraint, not inventing one.
insights.locator: And third, Deng Xiaoping announced the Four Cardinal Principles
